title: Ecosystems and Sustainability
seo_title: Grade 9 Science (SNC1W): Ecosystems and Sustainability Worksheets (Ontario)
standard_text: How matter cycles and energy flows keep ecosystems in dynamic equilibrium; how photosynthesis and cellular respiration balance each other; the role of biodiversity, air, water and soil quality and succession in sustainability; and how human activities affect ecosystems. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Science, Grade 9: SNC1W (2022), Strand B: Sustainable Ecosystems and Climate Change)
meta_desc: Free Grade 9 Science (SNC1W) worksheets on ecosystems and sustainability: food webs, energy pyramids, the carbon cycle, photosynthesis and respiration, biodiversity, succession and human impact. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Energy flows through an ecosystem; matter cycles round and round.
key_sub: Only about 10% of the energy passes to the next trophic level.
body_html:
How to think about it

Producers capture the Sun's energy in photosynthesis. Consumers get energy by eating, and at each trophic level most of the energy (about 90%) is used or lost as heat, so only about 10% passes on. That is why food chains are short and there are fewer top predators.

Matter is recycled: carbon moves between the air, living things, soil and oceans through photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition and combustion. Photosynthesis (CO₂ + H₂O → glucose + O₂) and cellular respiration (the reverse) balance each other. Biodiversity, healthy soil and clean water help an ecosystem recover from change.

Example

Producers store 10 000 J. How much energy reaches the secondary consumers?

10% to primary: 1000 J

10% to secondary: 100 J

Answer: about 100 J

Example

Which process returns carbon dioxide to the air?

Living things break down glucose for energy.

Answer: cellular respiration (also decomposition and burning)

Common mistakes

  • Saying energy is recycled: energy flows, matter cycles.
  • Drawing food-web arrows from the eater to the food: they point to the eater.
  • Thinking plants do not respire.

items.q: Where does most of the energy at each level go?
c: It stays stored forever in the top level.
It is recycled back to the producers.
It is lost as heat from respiration and in waste.
items.e: About 90% is used or lost each step.

items.q: The algae capture 2000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the snails?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 1 step.

items.q: Ava's energy pyramid shows 5000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?

Maya observes: “Bacteria in soil change nitrogen into a form plants can use.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Carbon from the air becomes part of the plant.
Nitrogen cycles from the soil into plants.
Carbon goes back into the air, where plants can take it in.
Matter and energy in the grass move into the rabbit.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Is energy recycled in an ecosystem?
c: No. Energy flows through and leaves as heat; matter is recycled.
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. A carbon atom in CO<sub>2</sub> enters a grass leaf. Which process?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

items.q: Where does formation of fossil fuels over millions of years move carbon?
c: from dead organisms into the geosphere
from living things into the atmosphere
from the geosphere into the atmosphere
items.e: Formation of fossil fuels over millions of years moves carbon from dead organisms into the geosphere.

items.q: Where does respiration move carbon?
c: from living things into the atmosphere
from the hydrosphere into the geosphere
from the geosphere into the atmosphere
items.e: Respiration moves carbon from living things into the atmosphere.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. A rabbit eats the grass. Then the rabbit releases the carbon as CO<sub>2</sub>. Which process?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

Nitrogen cycles from the soil into plants.
Carbon from the air becomes part of the plant.
Matter and energy in the grass move into the rabbit.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Which process moves carbon from producers into consumers?

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. A dead tree's carbon is released by fungi. Which process?

items.q: Where do the atoms in your body come from?

items.q: Where does photosynthesis move carbon?

items.q: Chloe asks where water fits in photosynthesis. Which is true?

It comes from the soil through the roots.

items.q: Benjamin reads: “A forest fire burns a large area.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Leah observes: “Cars and factories burn fossil fuels.” What impact can this have?

algae blooms that use up oxygen and kill fish

items.q: Kai wants to know whether a wildlife bridge reduces animal deaths. What is the best way to monitor this?

items.e: Monitoring uses measurements over time, before and after.

items.q: Jayden learns: Sea otters were overhunted. What happened to the sea urchins?
c: They increased and ate the kelp forests.
items.e: A change to one part of an ecosystem affects other populations.

items.q: Olivia learns: Zebra mussels spread in a lake. What happened to the native mussels?

items.e: A change to one part of an ecosystem affects other populations.

items.e: A good solution targets the cause of the impact.
